issues.legal_issue: A licensor may obtain an order for surrender of possession through a suit framed as a mandatory injunction after revoking a licence, where the suit is brought without considerable delay.
material_facts: The respondent occupied the shed under a one-year licence granted by the appellant.
The appellant revoked the licence before filing suit and sought an order directing the respondent to vacate.
The court found no considerable delay that would disentitle the appellant to discretionary relief.
issues.conclusion: The suit was effectively one for possession and should not fail merely because it was framed as a suit for mandatory injunction; the appellant was entitled to relief.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 55 of the Specific Relief Act, a licensee who fails to surrender possession after termination of the licence may be compelled to do so by mandatory injunction. Milka Singh v. Diana was relied on for the principle that a licensee remains a licensee after termination and must surrender possession. Although considerable delay may lead a court to refuse discretionary injunctive relief and require a separate possession suit, no such delay was shown here; avoiding multiplicity of suits also supported granting relief.

predicates.licensor_sues_after_license_revocation: The licensor filed a suit seeking the licensee's surrender of possession after revoking the licence.
predicates.licensee_has_not_surrendered_possession: The licensee continued to hold the property rather than surrendering it to the licensor.
predicates.no_considerable_delay: The licensor brought the suit without considerable delay after the licence was revoked.

issues.definition: When a licensor sues after revoking a licence, the licensee has not surrendered possession, and the suit was brought without considerable delay, the licensor may obtain surrender through a mandatory injunction.

issues.legal_issue: A licensee sued for possession after revocation cannot resist surrender by asserting title acquired from a person other than the licensor or someone lawfully claiming under the licensor, but may pursue that title separately.
material_facts: The respondent occupied the shed as the appellant's licensee, and the licence was revoked before the suit was filed.
After the suit was filed, the respondent purchased the property from its original owner.
The respondent had not surrendered possession to the appellant.
The respondent's asserted title was not acquired from the appellant or someone lawfully claiming under the appellant.
issues.conclusion: The respondent was required to surrender possession and pursue any title acquired from another person separately; the appellant was entitled to recover possession.
issues.legal_principle: The court applied the principle that a licensee remains a licensee and must surrender possession after revocation. It relied on Milka Singh v. Diana for that principle. It rejected the High Court's reliance on section 116 of the Indian Evidence Act to bar eviction in these circumstances. A later acquisition of title from a person other than the licensor or someone lawfully claiming under the licensor does not create a merger; title acquired from the licensor or such a claimant would be different because it could result in merger.

predicates.recovery_suit_follows_license_revocation: The licensor brought a suit to recover possession after revoking the defendant's licence.
predicates.licensee_has_not_surrendered_possession: The defendant remained in possession instead of surrendering the property to the licensor.
predicates.title_acquired_from_other_person: The defendant acquired the asserted title from someone other than the licensor or a person lawfully claiming under the licensor.

issues.definition: If a recovery suit follows revocation, the licensee has not surrendered possession, and the asserted title came from another person, the licensee must surrender possession before pursuing a separate title remedy.

issues.legal_issue: A sale of the leased property by its owner to the licensee does not merge or extinguish the tenant's continuing lease, and the tenant remains protected from eviction except through the applicable legal process.
material_facts: The appellant held a lease of the property from its original owner.
While the appellant's lease continued, the appellant granted the respondent a licence to occupy the shed.
After the suit was filed, the respondent purchased the entire property from its original owner.
The appellant's lease had not been lawfully terminated, and the applicable rent restriction regime limited eviction of the tenant.
issues.conclusion: The sale to the respondent did not merge or extinguish the appellant's lease; the lease continued, and the tenant could not be evicted except in accordance with the applicable law.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13 of the East Punjab Rent Restriction Act, 1949 protected the tenant from eviction except in accordance with that Act. The court held that the sale by the original owner to the licensee did not merge or extinguish the appellant's lease. It relied on K.K. Verma v. Union of India for the principle that a landlord must obtain eviction through lawful process.

predicates.tenant_holds_continuing_lease: The tenant held a lease that had not been terminated before the property was sold.
predicates.licensee_purchases_property_from_origina: A person occupying part of the property under the tenant's licence later purchased the property from its original owner.
predicates.tenancy_regime_restricts_eviction: The governing tenancy regime permits the tenant's eviction only through a specified legal process.

issues.definition: When a tenant holds a continuing lease, the licensee later purchases the property from its original owner, and the tenancy regime restricts eviction, the lease continues and eviction must follow lawful process.
